feedback.problem:
Let $V=C[0,1]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,1],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

If $x(t)={e}^{{t}^{2}}+k$ and $y(t)=t$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V,$ then $k=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are orthogonal, their inner product must be zero.

First, we compute the inner product using our definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{{t}^{2}}+k)t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+kt)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{{t}^{2}}}{2}+\frac{k{t}^{2}}{2}){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{e+k-1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set $⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=0$ and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x(t),y(t)⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{e+k-1}{2} & =0 \\ e+k-1 & =0 \\ k & =1-e\end{aligned}
$$
